newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila stocks seen declining steadily this week.
newsitem.headline: Manila stocks seen declining steadily this week.

text.p: Philippine shares will continue to drift down this week but are unlikely to repeat the savaging of last week when investors fled the market in droves, sparked by fears of a property collapse, analysts said.
Further falls will also put more pressure on the peso as foreign investors switch the proceeds of their share sales into dollars and take them elsewhere.
"It looks like there will be a steady drop as the market has adjusted to the bad news including those on specific companies," said Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities.

"A lot is sentiment-driven and I think it's going to continue. People may try to bottom fish in some stocks but overall, it's difficult to say," said Felix Barrientos, dealer at ING Baring Securities Phils Inc.
The main index finished the week almost 10 percent lower, hovering just above 2,600 after some of the sharpest falls the market has seen in more than two years.
It has plunged over 840 points, or 24 percent, since its record high just three months ago.
Analysts have traced the market's weakness to concerns that the property sector was headed for trouble which would spill over to the banking sector.
Poor first quarter corporate earnings, especially of firms such as Petron Corp and Manila Electric Co which are seen as a gauge of the economy, have raised fears of an economic slowdown.
The Philippine peso, hit in recent days by the stock market's plunge, could remain haunted by foreign funds moving out, bank traders said.
But traders said the peso was not likely to budge from 26.375 to the dollar after the Central Bank showed its resolve to defend the local currency.
Late Wednesday, the Central Bank flooded the market with dollars and raised its overnight borrowing rate by 0.75 percentage points to 11 percent to quell peso speculation.
"It's going to settle at this level (26.375)," said Antonio Agcaoili, treasurer of Banco Santander. "It was a very strong signal when the Central Bank raised its overnight rate."
"The Central Bank will always be there to protect the rate," said Monique Hugo, chief dealer of Standard Chartered Bank.

Earlier assurances from President Fidel Ramos that the Philippines was not headed for a property crash failed to soothe nerves at the bourse, any more than denials by property firms that they faced a glut.
Analysts said the market would test the immediate support of 2,600 next week and once broken may attempt to pierce the 2,200 level.
Sun Hung Kai Securities Phils vice-president Raul Ruiz said release of April inflation data next week was unlikely to bring cheer to the market.
However the United States' Federal Reserve Open Market Committee meeting on May 20 to decide whether to adjust interest rates may move the market.
Some analysts are counting on first quarter gross national product (GNP) growth, expected to be released the first week of June, to lift the market out of the doldrums. Others are not as confident.
"The outlook is still negative. We see no light yet at the end of the tunnel," said Teresa Lee, vice-president at Asiamerit Securities.
Though some stocks posted gains, including blue chip Metropolitan Bank & Trust Co and Meralco B, on Friday, analysts said any uptick in the near term would be technical.
